tldr: By mathematically formalizing evolving experimental states and the physical constraints of laboratory equipment, the authors built a framework that simulates and verifies chemistry experiment programs generated by LLM agents before running them on physical hardware.
hero_caption: An overall view of physical experimental procedures modeled as a computable state-transition system. By defining research object states (samples, containers, measurement data) and equipment operation contracts, complex experiments can be assembled without mathematical flaws using five operators: sequence, loop, branch, parallel fork-join, and protected interval.
overview:
Research on "Self-Driving Laboratories," where AI autonomously formulates hypotheses and runs experiments, is gaining momentum worldwide. Using large language models (LLMs), generating plausible-sounding experimental protocols in text is relatively easy. However, when attempting to execute those plans on physical robotic platforms, numerous failures occur: depleted samples, containers with lids left closed, equipment capacity overflows, and contradictions in physical ordering.

This study focuses on the gap between "chemically sound plans" and "physically executable plans." Conventional systems attempt to convert text-based protocols directly into hardware API calls. Because they cannot track how samples evolve during execution, they suffer from runtime errors and risk damaging instruments.

To address this, the authors devised a framework that represents the laboratory itself as a computable "state-transition system." They defined research objects as typed objects, constrained equipment actions through "skill contracts" with explicit preconditions and post-transformation effects, and designed a workflow algebra that composes these actions using five control flow operators.

Applying this methodology to a laboratory equipped with 45 physical workstations and 4 virtual modules, they demonstrated that fully verified executable programs with zero physical errors could be automatically generated from four complex catalyst and material synthesis prompts.
contributions: Proposed "Typed Research Objects" and a state-transition model that collectively manage samples, containers, and measurement data.
Formulated a "workflow algebra" guaranteeing physical consistency through five operators: sequence, bounded loop, conditional branch, parallel fork-join, and protected interval.
Implemented 49 workstation specifications (63 capabilities) as machine-readable skill contracts, establishing a safety pipeline with static analysis and stateful simulation prior to dispatch.
Demonstrated that an LLM agent could autonomously generate four complex experimental workflows without flaws, including catalyst synthesis and high-performance liquid/gas chromatography optimization.

sections.heading: Reframing the laboratory as a computable state-action space
sections.summary: Chemical experiments are formalized not as mere text protocols, but as a rigorous state-transition system. By defining the states of research samples and containers alongside equipment preconditions as types, physically non-executable plans can be eliminated in advance.
sections.details:
When running autonomous laboratory robots, the greatest obstacle is the plan failure where instructions "make sense as text, but are physically impossible to execute." Examples include pipetting liquid into a container whose lid remains closed, or reusing a sample that was completely depleted in an earlier step.

To solve this, the study rigorously models the laboratory as a state-transition system. The state of research objects at workflow step $t$ is defined as $S_t$. This $S_t$ maintains structured physical and historical information: not only sample substance name, mass, and volume, but also container type, lid status, physical location, and historical measurement data (such as pH or absorbance).

Meanwhile, each physical operation $f_i$ performed by robots or analytical instruments is defined as a function with parameters $\theta_i$. This function has a strictly specified precondition predicate $P_i$ that must be satisfied before execution. Only when $P_i(S_t, \theta_i) = 1$ is satisfied does the state transition to $S_{t+1}$ and new measurement data get recorded. If the conditions are not met, the simulated state does not change at all, and a specific error diagnosis is returned. The core innovation here is treating experimental operations not as black-box command calls, but as "state transformations governed by physical constraints."

sections.heading: A workflow algebra built on five operators
sections.summary: The authors established a "workflow algebra" to combine isolated experimental operations into complex protocols. Five operators—sequence, bounded loop, conditional branch, parallel fork-join, and protected interval—enable entire experimental procedures to be written as mathematically verifiable programs.
sections.details:
Even when individual operations are correctly defined, new inconsistencies can arise when chaining them into complete experimental procedures. To address this, the authors designed a workflow algebra with five primitive operators:

- Sequence ($F_{seq}$): Executes operations in serial order. The output state of the previous operation must strictly belong to the input domain of the subsequent operation.
- Bounded loop ($F_{loop}$): Repeats processing until a condition is satisfied. To prevent laboratory deadlocks from infinite loops, a finite maximum iteration limit $N_{max}$ is required. If the limit is reached without convergence, explicit diagnostic information is emitted.
- Conditional branch ($F_{cond}$): Branches based on measurement evidence. Branching conditions are mutually exclusive, ensuring that exactly one path is deterministically selected for any input.
- Parallel fork–join ($F_{par}$): Measures or processes aliquoted sub-samples from a single parent sample concurrently. Branches must have no write conflicts, and common updates must be consistent as a prerequisite for joining.
- Protected interval ($F_{lock}$): Executes sensitive processes sequentially on the scheduler without external interruption, preventing sample degradation during multi-step tasks such as electrode preparation.

These operators can be nested recursively. Consequently, experimental protocols are no longer free-form scripts, but structured programs verifiable on a computer as Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs). A major advantage is the complete separation between scientific hypothesis generation (what to test) and physical feasibility verification (how to run it).

sections.heading: Translating to hardware with pre-execution simulation
sections.summary: To execute formalized workflows on a real autonomous laboratory system, 49 workstation specifications were codified into "Function Skills." Furthermore, a "validate-then-commit" safety pipeline was implemented, combining AST static analysis with a stateful simulator.
sections.details:
Engineering work was conducted to bridge theory to a real robotic laboratory. The target self-driving laboratory includes diverse modules: liquid handling, heated stirring, centrifugation, XRD (X-ray diffraction), and GC (gas chromatography).

From 45 physical workstations and 4 virtual control modules (49 specifications total), the authors formalized 63 executable "Function Skills." Each skill encodes container geometry, capacity limits, required lid status, and temperature/pressure constraints as "MUST" (mandatory) or "SHOULD" (recommended) rules.

When an LLM agent receives a scientific intent and generates a Python workflow, the system performs a multi-stage validation check:

1. AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) static analysis: Blocks unauthorized library imports, dynamic code execution, and unregistered function calls, while normalizing the code (optimization levels O0 through O2).
2. Stateful Simulator: Virtually executes the code within a shared simulation environment. State changes are committed only if all MUST constraints pass at each step. If any violation occurs, the state is rolled back, and detailed error diagnostics (which step, which parameter, and what constraint was violated) are returned to the agent.

Through this mechanism, physical bugs in the program can be 100% caught before a robot spills reagents or crashes hardware.

captions.P4: Overall architecture of the modular autonomous laboratory (a) and the development framework from workstation skill formalization to agent generation and simulation verification (b, c). Agent-generated code is dispatched to physical hardware only after static optimization and stateful simulation.

sections.heading: Generating executable workflows from scientific intent
sections.summary: Automated workflow generation was evaluated across four advanced scientific tasks, including catalyst synthesis and analytical condition optimization. The LLM agent successfully generated complex procedures with branches and loops without contradictions, using only the provided list of skills.
sections.details:
To evaluate the generality and expressiveness of the system, workflows were generated from prompts containing only "scientific objectives and high-level control policies" without detailing workstation-level execution steps (using GPT-5.6 Sol as the LLM). Four tasks were evaluated:

- Fe introduction pathway comparison for NiFe catalysts: Synthesizing catalysts via five different routes and comparing oxygen evolution reaction (OER) performance in alkaline media. The agent produced a 27-node linear sequence spanning 11 workstations.
- Layered double hydroxide (LDH) synthesis and multi-modal analysis: Synthesizing LDH catalysts and fabricating electrodes inside a protected interval (9 steps). Following HMF oxidation, solid electrodes and liquid products were branched in parallel across three analytical paths (contact angle, XRD, liquid chromatography) before joining, forming a 22-node (31 simulation steps) procedure across 11 instruments.
- Closed-loop optimization of furfural hydrogenation and GC conditions: A 20-node (23 steps) procedure containing a bounded loop (maximum iterations $N_{max} = 6$) that dynamically adjusted gas chromatography conditions until peak resolution met target thresholds.
- ZnO nanoparticle synthesis with adaptive dilution measurement: A 27-node (30 steps, 15 instruments) procedure combining parallel FTIR/UV-vis measurements with a dilution loop ($N_{max} = 3$) that repeated until absorbance fell within the linear quantitation range (0.20–1.00 AU).

Importantly, these workflows were not rigid templates; the agent assembled them autonomously to satisfy state-transition requirements. All four workflows passed simulation with zero MUST errors and zero SHOULD warnings.

sections.heading: From protocol-centric to state-centric autonomous experimentation
sections.summary: While existing research has focused mainly on translating text protocols, this work unifies object states, a workflow algebra, and executable skills. Localized failures can be isolated to specific objects and conditions, providing a foundation for long-horizon autonomous experiments.
sections.details:
Recent years have seen many software frameworks and ontologies proposed for autonomous laboratories. However, most conventional approaches have remained "procedure-centric" or "device-centric," focusing on how to represent text protocols or how schedulers manage instrument availability.

The decisive difference in this study is placing the evolving "Object state" at the center of the computational model. Across all phases—workflow generation, composition, and simulation verification—the current state of the sample is continuously tracked. As a result, if a plan has an issue, the system does not simply reject the entire script; it provides pinpointed feedback, such as "Container A exceeded capacity at step 3" or "pH condition was not met when loop 4 hit its bound."

Of course, current simulations depend on the completeness of defined skill contracts and cannot predict unexpected hardware failures or unknown chemical reaction byproducts. Nevertheless, constraints and state definitions can be expanded over time. Placing such a rigorous "computable interface" between agent reasoning and physical transformations is the most reliable path toward true autonomous scientific discovery.

sections.heading: Technical details of implementation and evaluation
sections.summary: This section details the internal structure of typed objects, the 100-point rubric for converting natural-language specs into skills, the multi-stage AST optimizer, and the simulator's error-handling architecture.
sections.details:
Key technical details of the system implementation are summarized below.

### Implementation of Research Objects and Skills
While conceptual state $S$ holds extensive sample composition and history, the simulated `SimStatet` strictly tracks attributes necessary for verification: container ID, container type, lid status, sample state, liquid volume, mass, and current physical location. Eleven container types are defined, including sample vials and 96-well plates. Workstation specifications written in natural language are evaluated using a 100-point rubric consisting of mandatory criteria (60 points) and optional criteria (40 points). Specifications scoring 60 points or higher are compiled into formal Function Skills.

### AST Optimization and Simulation
Python scripts generated by the agent are passed to `recipe_optimizer.py`. Unsafe system calls are blocked by a security gate (O0), followed by canonicalization (O1) and safe syntactic simplification (O2) before reaching the simulator. The simulator evaluates the MUST conditions of each operation, updating state only upon success. On failure, it generates an `ErrorEntry` (function name, step number, error code, expected value, observed value, and remediation suggestion) to feed back to the agent.

### Experimental Prompts and Evaluation Setup
In the four validation tasks, prompts provided the agent (GPT-5.6 Sol) with goals and logical conditions without explicit instrument execution steps. Generated code was serialized into JSON and AST representations to calculate node counts and execution steps. Because this paper focuses on establishing the representation formalisms and simulation verification, empirical data from physical wet-lab executions was not collected.

takeaways: When driving laboratory robots with LLMs, formalizing operations as a "state-transition system" with pre-execution verification is far more reliable than directly executing natural-language protocols.

Defining a workflow algebra with five primitive operators (sequence, bounded loop, conditional branch, parallel fork-join, protected interval) mathematically ensures the physical consistency of complex experiments.
Introducing a "validate-then-commit" simulator with structured error diagnostics enables a closed-loop environment where agents can autonomously correct their own code.
limitations: The four case studies presented in this paper were evaluated up to simulation verification; wet-lab experimental results moving physical reagents on hardware and real-time handling of physical hardware faults were not reported.
Simulator verification accuracy depends entirely on the completeness of human-authored workstation constraints (skill contracts).
The simulator cannot track or guarantee unmodeled chemical phenomena, such as unexpected precipitation or rapid exothermic reactions.
